- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is positive (≥0.67) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward more aggressively.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” decay to forecast slope.
- When sentiment shifts from positive to negative, model often lags in adjusting downward; add a lagged correction term (e.g., 1–2 days delay in downward revision).
- If model shows strong upward trend (e.g., >0.5% daily increase) with low sentiment, it’s prone to over-optimism; cap forecast growth at 0.3–0.4% per day.
- Mean reversion is stronger in low-sentiment periods; if sentiment is neutral or negative, forecast should revert toward 30-day moving average.
- In high-sentiment periods, model often underestimates volatility; increase forecast variance or add a 1–2% buffer for downside risk.
- If true outcome deviates >10% from 30-day MA, check sentiment history for “sentiment reversal” — if sentiment flips from positive to negative, model may be misaligned with new trend.
